chefNotes.text: Rice that has been chilled overnight has dried and firmed. Fresh rice carries surface moisture that steams at 100 °C and clumps.
chefNotes.title: Cold, day-old rice

chefNotes.text: Rendering the sausage first coats the wok in sweet, cured pork fat, which flavours every grain. That's why the dish needs no soy.
chefNotes.title: Lap cheong fat is the seasoning

chefNotes.text: Classic Yangzhou rice is seasoned with salt and white pepper, so it stays golden and white. Soy sauce would darken it and mask the shrimp.
chefNotes.title: Keep it pale

chefNotes.text: A home burner can't keep a full wok hot. Fry 2 portions at a time at most, or the rice steams rather than fries.
chefNotes.title: Batch for a home burner

name: Yangzhou Fried Rice with Lap Cheong
pairing: Jasmine or oolong tea, or a crisp lager.

steps.body:
Break the cold rice apart with wet hands so every grain is separate.
Blanch the carrot in boiling water until just tender, adding the peas for the last 30 seconds. Drain well.
steps.title: Prep and break up the rice

steps.body:
Fry the sausage in a dry wok over medium heat until the fat runs and the edges turn translucent.
Lift it out and leave the fat in the wok.
steps.title: Render the lap cheong

steps.body:
Turn the heat to high. Toss the mushrooms and shrimp until the shrimp just curl and turn pink.
Splash in the Shaoxing wine, then lift everything out.
steps.title: Sear the shrimp and mushrooms

steps.body:
Add the oil and pour in the eggs.
Scramble into soft, loose curds; don't let them set dry.
steps.title: Scramble the egg

steps.body:
Add the rice straight onto the egg.
Press and toss over high heat until the grains are hot, dry and hopping in the wok.
steps.title: Fry the rice

steps.body:
Return the sausage, shrimp, mushrooms, carrot and peas with the scallion whites.
Season with salt and white pepper and toss for 1 minute, then fold in the scallion greens.
steps.title: Combine and season

summary: Day-old rice is wok-fried in rendered lap cheong fat with soft egg, shrimp, carrot, peas, mushroom and scallion. Salt and white pepper, not soy, keep it pale.

why.text: Chilled rice dries and firms up, so the grains separate and fry instead of steaming into clumps.
why.title: Day-old rice

why.text: High heat browns the rice and gives it the smoky wok flavour.
why.title: Very hot wok

chefNotes.text: Cumin's aroma is released by fat and heat. Cracked seeds give the crunchy, street-stall crust that ground cumin alone can't.
chefNotes.title: Toast and crack the cumin

chefNotes.text: Xinjiang stalls thread a cube of lamb fat between every few pieces. It bastes the lean meat and crisps at the edges, so keep the fat on the shoulder.
chefNotes.title: Fat is part of the skewer

chefNotes.text: Spice added at the start carries the flavour, and the final dusting on the hot fat blooms fresh aroma. That second hit is the signature.
chefNotes.title: Dust twice

chefNotes.text: Over charcoal, or on a barbecue at full heat, cook 6–8 minutes, turning often. The char adds the smoky note the air fryer can't.
chefNotes.title: Charcoal adds the smoke

name: Xinjiang Cumin Lamb Skewers
pairing: A cold lager, or Syrah.

photo.alt: Three cumin-crusted lamb skewers on cilantro with cucumber slices

serveWith: Flatbread or naan, smashed cucumber and pickled red onion.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Xinjiang Lamb Skewers · omnivorescookbook.com

steps.body:
Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan until fragrant and a shade darker.
Crack half and grind the rest, then mix with the chilli, Sichuan pepper, salt and sugar.
steps.title: Make the spice mix

steps.body:
Toss the lamb with the grated onion, Shaoxing wine, soy, potato starch, 1 tbsp oil and a third of the spice mix.
Cover and refrigerate for at least an hour, or overnight.
steps.title: Marinate

steps.body:
Thread the lamb tightly onto the skewers, alternating lean and fatty pieces.
Brush with the rest of the oil and press on half the remaining spice mix.
steps.title: Skewer

steps.body:
Air-fry at 200 °C, turning once, until browned at the edges.
Go by temperature: 63 °C in the centre for medium, or up to 70 °C for shoulder that's tender and juicy.
steps.title: Air-fry

steps.body:
While the skewers are still sizzling, dust them with the last of the spice mix so it blooms in the fat.
Serve on a bed of cilantro with cucumber rounds.
steps.title: Dust and serve

summary: Lamb shoulder is marinated with grated onion and Shaoxing, threaded tight and air-fried under a toasted cumin, chilli and Sichuan pepper rub. A second dusting goes on while the skewers are still hot.

why.text: Pieces of fat on each skewer baste the lean lamb as it grills.
why.title: Fat between the meat

why.text: Ground cumin and chilli burn if they go on too early, so they're added after the first char.
why.title: Spice once it chars

chefNotes.text: The aromatics in the paste are fat-soluble. Frying them in cracked coconut fat is where the depth comes from; simmering paste in milk alone tastes raw.
chefNotes.title: Fry the paste until the oil breaks

chefNotes.text: Collagen-rich thigh stays juicy in a simmer, while breast goes stringy. Go by thermometer: 74 °C is safe, but thigh texture peaks higher.
chefNotes.title: Thighs, to 80–85 °C

chefNotes.text: Pound in a few cilantro roots, a little extra garlic and 2 fresh green chillies. Jarred paste loses its fresh-herb top notes.
chefNotes.title: Upgrade a jarred paste

chefNotes.text: Half a lime squeezed in at the end lifts the coconut richness without adding salt.
chefNotes.title: Finish with acid if it's heavy

name: Thai Green Curry Chicken
pairing: Off-dry, lower-alcohol Riesling, or a Thai iced tea or lime soda with no alcohol.

serveWith: Jasmine rice and a quick cucumber salad.

steps.body: Simmer the coconut cream in a wok or the braiser over medium heat, stirring, until the oil separates and it looks curdled and glossy.
steps.title: Crack the cream

steps.body:
Add the curry paste and lime leaves and fry in the coconut oil, stirring constantly.
It's ready when it darkens slightly, smells intensely fragrant and oil pools at the edges.
steps.title: Fry the paste

steps.body: Add the chicken and stir until it's coated and opaque on the outside. Don't brown it.
steps.title: Coat the chicken

steps.body:
Pour in the coconut milk and stock and add the mushrooms.
Keep it at a gentle simmer, not a boil, so the coconut stays silky. Cook until the thighs reach 80 °C.
steps.title: Simmer

steps.body:
Off the heat, add the fish sauce and palm sugar.
Taste: salty first, then gently sweet, with clear heat. Adjust with fish sauce before adding more sugar.
steps.title: Season

steps.body:
Stir in the chilli and half the mint.
Ladle into shallow bowls, top with the rest of the mint, the cilantro and the scallions, and serve with jasmine rice.
steps.title: Finish and serve

summary: This brothy gaeng keow wan gai fries green paste in cracked coconut cream, then simmers thighs in coconut milk lengthened with chicken stock. Fish sauce, palm sugar, bird's eye chilli, mint and cilantro finish it.

why.text: Frying the paste in coconut cream until the fat separates blooms the aromatics.
why.title: Crack the coconut cream

why.text: Season with fish sauce, then balance with palm sugar. That's the Thai order of seasoning.
why.title: Salt first, then sweet

chefNotes.text: The starch gelatinises into the elastic, slightly bouncy skin of a breakfast stall. Flour alone makes a soft French crêpe.
chefNotes.title: Tapioca is the chew

chefNotes.text: Ten minutes lets the flour hydrate, so the skin swirls thin and won't tear when you flip it.
chefNotes.title: Rest the batter

chefNotes.text: This is what non-stick is for. Medium heat sets the egg before the skin dries out, and gives that freckled gold without browning it hard.
chefNotes.title: A non-stick pan at medium heat

chefNotes.text: Cook a stack of plain skins, interleave them with parchment and freeze. They go straight from the freezer onto the egg.
chefNotes.title: Make-ahead skins

name: Taiwanese Dan Bing
pairing: Hot or iced soy milk, or a black milk tea.

photo.alt: Two rolled Taiwanese egg crepes with golden egg, lacy edges and black sesame

serveWith: Warm soy milk (doujiang), or Taiwanese milk tea.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Dan Bing (Taiwanese Egg Crepes) · tiffycooks.com

steps.body:
Whisk the flour, tapioca starch, salt and water into a thin, lump-free batter, about as thick as milk.
Stir in half the scallion and rest it so the flour hydrates.
steps.title: Mix and rest the batter

steps.body: Beat each egg in its own bowl with a pinch of salt and white pepper and the rest of the scallion.
steps.title: Beat the eggs

steps.body:
Heat a 24–26 cm non-stick pan over medium with a little oil.
Stir the batter, pour in half and swirl it thin.
It's ready when the top turns from milky to translucent and the edges go lacy and lift.
steps.title: Cook the skin

steps.body:
Flip the skin. Pour one egg into the pan beside it, then lay the skin straight back over the egg.
Press it lightly and cook until the egg sets and freckles gold.
steps.title: Fuse the egg

steps.body:
Flip so the egg is on top and scatter with black sesame. Add any filling, then roll it up tightly in the pan.
Cut it in two, or into 5 pieces stall-style, and serve with soy paste.
Repeat for the second crepe.
steps.title: Roll and slice

summary: The breakfast-stall egg crepe fries a scallion egg onto a thin, chewy flour-and-tapioca skin, then rolls it up. Black sesame and soy paste finish it.

why.text: A thin flour batter fries into a chewy-crisp wrapper, and the egg on top makes it tender.
why.title: Thin batter, then egg

chefNotes.text: Blood proteins and scum would cloud the braise and taste muddy. A 10-minute blanch and rinse gives a clean, glossy sauce.
chefNotes.title: Blanch first

chefNotes.text: Caramelised rock sugar gives the deep mahogany colour and sticky gloss that soy alone can't. It's milder and rounder than white sugar.
chefNotes.title: Rock sugar is the lacquer

chefNotes.text: Trotter skin and tendon are mostly collagen, which melts into gelatin over 2 hours at 85–90 °C. That gives the lip-sticking texture, and the sauce sets to jelly overnight.
chefNotes.title: Collagen is the point

chefNotes.text: Drop peeled soft-boiled eggs into the braise for the last 30 minutes. They come out as soy-stained lu dan for the bento.
chefNotes.title: Add eggs for lu dan

name: Taiwanese Braised Pork Knuckle Rice
pairing: Oolong tea or a cold Taiwan Beer.

photo.alt: Taiwanese braised pork knuckle with rice, peanuts, pickled daikon, cucumber and braised shiitake in a green bento plate

serveWith: Jasmine rice, pickled daikon, cucumber and blanched greens. A lu dan makes it a full bento.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Taiwanese Braised Pork Hock · tiffycooks.com

steps.body:
Cover the pork with cold water, bring it to the boil and blanch to purge the scum.
Drain, rinse, and shave off any stray hairs.
steps.title: Blanch the pork

steps.body:
In the braiser over medium heat, melt the rock sugar in the oil until it turns deep amber.
Add the pork and toss until every piece is lacquered.
steps.title: Caramelise the rock sugar

steps.body:
Add the ginger, scallions, star anise, cinnamon and five-spice.
Splash the Shaoxing around the hot edge, then add both soy sauces, the shiitake, peanuts and water. The liquid should almost cover the pork.
steps.title: Build the braise

steps.body:
Bring to a bare tremble, cover, and braise on the lowest burner, turning once or twice.
It's done when the skin is sticky and a chopstick slides into the meat.
steps.title: Braise low

steps.body:
Uncover and simmer until the liquid is glossy and coats the pork.
Taste, then adjust with soy or sugar.
steps.title: Reduce the sauce

steps.body:
Spoon rice into each plate and drizzle it with the braising sauce and a few peanuts.
Add the pork, shiitake, pickled daikon and cucumber, then finish with cilantro and scallion greens.
steps.title: Plate bento-style

summary: Zhu jiao fan lacquers blanched pork knuckle in caramelised rock sugar, then braises it with soy, Shaoxing and five-spice until the skin turns sticky. It's served bento-style over sauced rice with peanuts, shiitake, pickled daikon and cucumber.

why.text: It gives the braise its mahogany colour and gloss.
why.title: Caramelise the rock sugar

why.text: Hours of braising melt the skin's collagen into a sticky sauce that coats the rice.
why.title: Collagen makes the sauce

chefNotes.text: Starting cold lets the thick fat cap melt out before the meat overheats. A hot pan seizes the skin and leaves a rubbery fat layer.
chefNotes.title: Cold pan, slow render

chefNotes.text: Chefs serve duck breast rosy at about 57 °C. Health Canada's poultry minimum is 74 °C, so cook to that for vulnerable guests; it'll be firmer and grey.
chefNotes.title: Pull at a rosy 57 °C

chefNotes.text: A breast gives off 60–80 ml of fat. Strain it into a jar and use it for roast potatoes or the Double Soup Shoyu Ramen aroma oil. It keeps for months in the fridge.
chefNotes.title: Bank the duck fat

chefNotes.text: Orange is the classic duck partner because its acid and sweetness balance the fat. A quick pan sauce works too: deglaze with orange juice, reduce, and mount with butter.
chefNotes.title: Citrus cuts the richness

items.note: zest and a squeeze of juice

name: Seared Duck Breast with Mash and Asparagus
pairing: Pinot Noir, or Nebbiolo for a bigger red.

serveWith: Riced potato mash and asparagus, or a bitter-leaf salad in winter.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Pan-Seared Duck Breasts · americastestkitchen.com

steps.body:
Score the skin in a tight crosshatch, through the fat but not into the meat.
Pat dry, season all over and rest uncovered.
steps.title: Score and salt the duck

steps.body: Start the potatoes in cold salted water and simmer until a knife slides through.
steps.title: Boil the potatoes

steps.body:
Lay the breasts skin-down in a cold, dry pan, then set it over medium-low heat.
Render slowly, pouring off and saving the fat as it builds, until the skin is thin, deep brown and crisp.
steps.title: Render skin-side down

steps.body:
Flip and cook the flesh side for 1–2 minutes, to 54 °C in the thickest part.
Rest skin-up. It carries over to a rosy 57 °C.
steps.title: Finish and rest

steps.body:
Toss the asparagus in 1 tbsp of the duck fat with salt.
Roast at 220 °C, or air-fry at 200 °C, until tender-crisp and blistered. Finish with a squeeze of lemon.
steps.title: Roast the asparagus

steps.body:
Drain the potatoes and let them steam-dry for 1 minute.
Rice them, beat in the butter and warm milk, season, and finish with cracked pepper.
steps.title: Mash

steps.body:
Slice the duck 1 cm thick on the bias and fan it over the mash with the asparagus alongside.
Finish with orange zest, a squeeze of orange and a pinch of shichimi.
steps.title: Slice and serve

summary: A cold-pan start renders the duck skin thin and crisp while the meat rests to a rosy 57 °C. It's served over buttery mash with asparagus roasted in the duck fat, orange zest and shichimi.

why.text: Slow heat renders the thick fat layer so the skin crisps before the meat overcooks.
why.title: Start skin-down in a cold pan

chefNotes.text: A crosshatch on the inside of the body makes it curl into a pinecone and cook in 60–90 seconds. Any longer and it turns rubbery.
chefNotes.title: Score the squid

chefNotes.text: The katsuobushi brings inosinate and the kombu brings glutamate. The chashu and shiitake add more, which is why this light broth still tastes rich.
chefNotes.title: Dashi plus pork is double umami

chefNotes.text: It's flash-frozen at its best chew and needs only a minute in boiling water. T&T stocks it.
chefNotes.title: Frozen sanuki udon beats fresh or dried

chefNotes.text: The broth is plain dashi seasoned as kakejiru (see Dashi Stock). Only the chashu, eggs and shiitake carry over from a Double Soup Shoyu Ramen batch.
chefNotes.title: Dashi broth, not ramen soup

pairing: A cold Japanese lager, or hot genmaicha.

serveWith: Rice balls or a small side of pickles.
source: Johnew's own recipe · broth is my Dashi Stock; chashu and egg from my Double Soup Shoyu Ramen

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Nabeyaki Udon · justonecookbook.com

steps.body:
Put the kombu and water in a saucepan over medium heat and bring it slowly to a steaming, gentle simmer. Don't let it boil.
Lift out the kombu at about 80 °C, as the first bubbles form; boiled kombu turns slimy and bitter.
steps.title: Heat the kombu slowly

steps.body:
Turn off the heat, sprinkle in the bonito flakes and steep for 5 minutes.
Strain into a clean saucepan without pressing, then discard the bonito. This is the same as my Dashi Stock.
steps.title: Infuse and strain

steps.body:
Add the light soy, mirin and salt and keep it just below a simmer.
Taste: it should be gently seasoned and sippable.
steps.title: Season the kakejiru

steps.body: Soak the wakame in cold water until it unfurls, then drain.
steps.title: Rehydrate the wakame

steps.body:
Drop the squid and shrimp into the barely simmering broth.
Cook until the shrimp turn pink and the scored squid curls into a pinecone, 60–90 seconds. Don't go longer, or it toughens.
steps.title: Poach the seafood

steps.body:
Torch or pan-sear the chashu, and warm the eggs and shiitake in the broth for a minute.
Cook the udon in boiling water for about 1 minute until loose, then drain.
steps.title: Warm the toppings and udon

steps.body:
Put the udon in hot bowls and ladle the broth and seafood over.
Arrange the chashu, eggs, shiitake and wakame around the edge, pile scallion and cilantro in the centre, and finish with shichimi and black sesame.
steps.title: Assemble

summary: Thick sanuki udon sits in a clear kakejiru made from my Dashi Stock, with poached scored squid and shrimp. Rolled chashu, ajitama, braised shiitake, wakame, shichimi and black sesame top it.

why.text: Clean dashi umami lets the seafood and chashu stand out instead of competing with a heavy broth.
why.title: Dashi as the base

chefNotes.text: Boiling emulsifies the fat and clouds the broth; low heat keeps it clear and golden.
chefNotes.title: Keep it at a low simmer

chefNotes.text: Most foam rises in the first 10 minutes after the boil; skim it then and the broth stays clean.
chefNotes.title: Skim early

chefNotes.text: A 5 cm piece steeped in the strained broth off the heat adds glutamate for deeper umami.
chefNotes.title: Add a strip of kombu

chefNotes.text: With no salt in the broth, you can season each soup to taste, and the broth can go into ramen, rice or braises without over-salting.
chefNotes.title: An unseasoned broth is more useful

items.note: sliced; Vidalia or similar, or yellow onion

name: Samukichi's Golden Chicken Stock
pairing: Hot genmaicha or a crisp lager.

photo.alt: Bowl of golden chicken stock with tender chicken thigh pieces and carrot

region: Japanese chef's method · golden chicken soup
serveWith: Steamed rice, or over noodles.

sourceLinks.label: Stop Boiling Chicken Soup Like This (video) · youtube.com

steps.body:
Pat the thighs dry. Don't salt them, since the broth stays unseasoned.
Lay them skin-side down in a cold, dry pot, then turn the heat to medium. The fat renders out as the pot heats, and the skin goes golden without sticking.
steps.title: Brown from a cold pot

steps.body:
Add the onion and garlic and fry in the chicken fat until fragrant and lightly golden.
Add the carrot chunk and fry a little longer for more flavour, then add the celery leaves.
steps.title: Fry the aromatics

steps.body:
Pour in the water and add the thyme and bay. Bring to a boil over medium heat, then turn it to low.
Simmer gently, skimming foam as needed, until the thickest part of the thighs reads 80–85 °C.
steps.title: Add water and simmer the chicken

steps.body: Lift out the chicken and pull the meat off in large pieces. Set the meat aside.
steps.title: Take the meat off the bones

steps.body: Return the bones and skin to the pot and simmer on low for another 30–40 minutes, topping up with water if needed.
steps.title: Simmer the bones

steps.body: Strain through a fine sieve and keep only the clear golden broth. Leave it unseasoned.
steps.title: Strain for clear broth

steps.body:
Bring the broth back to a simmer, adding water if needed, and cook the carrot and celery until tender.
Return the chicken to warm through, season with salt and pepper to your liking, and finish with dried parsley. Serve as is or over noodles.
steps.title: Make the soup

summary: Skin-on thighs brown from a cold pot, then onion, garlic, carrot and celery leaves fry in the fat before the water goes in. The meat comes out once just cooked, the bones simmer on, and the strained clear broth becomes the base for soup.

why.text: Starting cold renders the skin's fat slowly, so it fries itself golden in its own fat and builds a fond for the broth.
why.title: Cold-pot browning

why.text: Onion, garlic and carrot browned in the fat add sweet, roasted depth before any water goes in.
why.title: Fry the aromatics in chicken fat

why.text: Thigh meat is tender at 80–85 °C and dries out with longer cooking, so it comes out while the bones keep giving flavour.
why.title: Meat out, bones in

chefNotes.text: Salt draws moisture out and then reabsorbs it, leaving a dry surface that browns instead of steaming.
chefNotes.title: Dry-brine for crisp skin

chefNotes.text: Sugar on chicken skin burns before the skin crisps. Glazing only the figs and onion keeps the skin crackly.
chefNotes.title: Glaze the fruit, not the skin

chefNotes.text: If it tastes heavy, finish with a squeeze of lemon rather than more salt.
chefNotes.title: Acid keeps figs from cloying

chefNotes.text: Under-ripe figs need another teaspoon of honey and 5 more minutes in the oven.
chefNotes.title: Firm figs need help

name: Roast Chicken Thighs with Figs
pairing: Pinot Noir or Grenache.

photo.alt: Two halves of a fresh purple fig, cut side up, in a small patterned dish

serveWith: Couscous or crusty bread, with a lemony arugula salad.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Chicken Thighs with Fresh Figs · America's Test Kitchen

steps.body:
Pat the thighs dry and season all over with the salt and pepper.
Refrigerate uncovered, skin-up, for at least 1 hour or overnight so the skin dries.
steps.title: Dry-brine

steps.body:
Heat the oven to 220 °C.
Warm the oil in the braiser over medium heat and lay the thighs in skin-down. Leave them until the skin is deep golden and the fat has rendered.
steps.title: Render the skin

steps.body:
Turn the thighs skin-up and tuck the onion, garlic and thyme into the fat around them.
Roast uncovered.
steps.title: First roast

steps.body:
Whisk the balsamic, honey and Dijon.
Nestle the figs cut-side up between the thighs, then spoon the glaze over the figs and onion, not the skin.
Roast until the figs slump and the thickest thigh reads 82 °C.
steps.title: Add the figs and glaze

steps.body:
Rest 5 minutes.
Spoon the jammy pan juices over the chicken and scatter with the walnuts and fresh thyme.
steps.title: Rest and finish

summary: Crisp-skinned bone-in thighs roast with fresh figs, red onion and thyme until the figs slump into the pan juices. A balsamic-honey glaze on the fruit keeps the sweetness in check.

why.text: Balsamic and Dijon keep the jammy figs from tasting cloying.
why.title: Figs need acid

why.text: Thyme's savoury, woodsy notes go with both sweet fruit and roast chicken.
why.title: Thyme bridges fruit and chicken

chefNotes.text: Deep browning on the oxtail and the fried tomato paste give the braise its Maillard depth. A pale sear makes a thin, winey sauce.
chefNotes.title: The fond is the sauce

chefNotes.text: Collagen starts converting to gelatin around 70 °C and goes faster near 82 °C. A liquid held at 85–90 °C gets there over 3 hours without boiling the meat fibres tight and dry.
chefNotes.title: Tremble, don't boil

chefNotes.text: Chill it overnight. The fat sets into a lid you can lift off, the meat reabsorbs the liquor, and the sauce tastes deeper. Reheat to 74 °C in the braiser.
chefNotes.title: Make it a day ahead

chefNotes.text: Fresh mint cuts the richness the way gremolata does on osso buco. Lemon zest also works if you'd rather keep it classic.
chefNotes.title: Mint as the lift

name: Red Wine Braised Oxtail
pairing: Syrah or Nebbiolo, served no warmer than 18 °C.

photo.alt: Glossy red wine braised oxtail with carrots and torn mint in a dark bowl

region: Queue de bœuf au vin rouge
serveWith: Creamy mash, soft polenta or crusty bread to mop up the glaze.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Red Wine-Braised Oxtails · sunset.com

steps.body:
Season the oxtail with salt and dust it lightly with flour.
Brown it hard in the oil in the braiser over medium-high heat, in batches, until it's deep mahogany on all sides. Set aside.
steps.title: Salt and brown

steps.body:
Lower the heat and cook the onion, celery and garlic in the fat until soft.
Stir in the tomato paste and fry until it turns brick red.
steps.title: Soften the aromatics

steps.body: Pour in the wine, scrape up the fond, and boil until it's reduced by half and the raw alcohol smell has gone.
steps.title: Deglaze

steps.body:
Return the oxtail with the stock, thyme, rosemary and bay. The liquid should come about three-quarters of the way up the meat.
Bring to a bare tremble, cover, and braise in a 150 °C oven.
steps.title: Braise

steps.body: Tuck in the carrots and continue uncovered. It's done when a fork slides into the oxtail without resistance and the carrots are tender.
steps.title: Add the carrots

steps.body:
Lift out the meat and carrots. Skim the fat, then reduce the liquor on the stove until syrupy and glossy.
Spoon it back over and scatter with torn mint.
steps.title: Glaze and serve

summary: Oxtail is browned hard and braised low in red wine, stock and tomato paste until it falls off the bone. Carrots join for the last hour, and the reduced liquor glazes the plate with mint on top.

steps.body:
Each spec is per drink. Stir and serve exactly as above.
- Bourbon (house): 60 ml bourbon, 7.5 ml rich demerara syrup, 2 Angostura + 1 orange bitters, orange peel. Vanilla and caramel.
- Rye: 60 ml rye, 5 ml syrup, 2 Angostura + 1 orange bitters, lemon and orange peel. Spicier and drier.
- Japanese whisky: 60 ml Japanese blended whisky, 5 ml syrup, 2 orange bitters, lemon peel. Light and floral.
- Smoky Scotch: 45 ml blended Scotch + 15 ml Islay single malt, 7.5 ml honey syrup (2:1), 2 Angostura, lemon peel. Peat and honey.
- Aged rum: 60 ml aged rum (Appleton 12 or El Dorado 12), 5 ml syrup, 2 Angostura + 1 orange bitters, orange peel. Molasses and spice.
- Oaxaca: 45 ml reposado tequila + 15 ml mezcal, 5 ml agave syrup, 2 Angostura, flamed orange peel. Phil Ward's 2007 modern classic.
- Cognac: 60 ml VSOP Cognac, 5 ml syrup, 2 Peychaud's + 1 Angostura, lemon peel. Dried fruit, close to a Sazerac.
- Zero-proof: 90 ml strong cold-brewed black tea (half Lapsang Souchong, half Assam), 7.5 ml syrup, 3 dashes alcohol-free bitters, orange peel.
steps.title: Choose your spirit

Heat a frying pan over high heat until it smokes, add the oil, then turn it down to medium.
Fry the strips in batches if needed, 2–3 minutes a side, until just cooked through. Lift them out.
steps.title: Fry the salmon

steps.body:
Wipe most of the oil from the pan.
Add the teriyaki sauce and squeeze in the juice from the grated ginger.
Simmer until slightly thickened and glossy.
steps.title: Reduce the glaze

steps.body:
Return the salmon, turn it once and spoon the sauce over for about a minute.
Plate it, scatter with scallion and serve with rice.
steps.title: Glaze and serve

summary: Starch-dusted salmon strips are pan-fried, then glazed in Adam Liaw's four-ingredient teriyaki of soy, mirin, sake and sugar. Ginger juice sharpens the glaze, and scallion finishes it.

why.text: Mirin and sugar burn fast, so the sauce goes in once the fish is nearly cooked and reduces to a gloss without scorching.
why.title: Glaze goes in last

why.text: Alcohol carries aroma and then cooks off; mirin's sugars give teriyaki its shine.
why.title: Sake and mirin

chefNotes.text: Cold eggs into boiling water make 6 minutes repeatable; give extra-large eggs 6½.
chefNotes.title: Always start fridge-cold

chefNotes.text: A sheet of paper towel over the top keeps the eggs under the marinade so they colour evenly.
chefNotes.title: Keep them submerged

chefNotes.text: The braising liquid from the Double Soup Shoyu Ramen is the original cure and seasons them best.
chefNotes.title: Use your chashu liquid

chefNotes.text: The yolks stay soft, below Health Canada's 74 °C for egg dishes.
chefNotes.title: Pasteurised for vulnerable guests

pairing: A cold Japanese lager or a dry junmai sake.

serveWith: Halved on ramen or udon, or on its own with rice and a little of the marinade.
source: Converted from Adam Liaw · Ramen School 003

sourceLinks.label: Ramen School 003: Ajitama (Ramen Eggs) · adamliaw.com

steps.body:
Prick a small hole in the base of each egg.
Lower into boiling water, reduce to a simmer and cook 6 minutes.
steps.title: Prick and boil

steps.body: Move the eggs straight into iced water and cool completely, then peel.
steps.title: Ice them

steps.body:
Mix the chashu braising liquid with the water.
For the alternative, bring the mirin and sake to a boil and flame off the alcohol, then add the soy, water and any aromatics.
steps.title: Make the marinade

steps.body:
Submerge the peeled eggs in the marinade and refrigerate for 2 days.
They keep about 4 days, in or out of the liquid.
steps.title: Cure 48 hours

steps.body: Halve with a wet knife, or with string or fishing line the way ramen shops do, so the jammy yolk doesn't drag.
steps.title: Slice

summary: Six-minute eggs cure for 48 hours in chashu braising liquid, or in a soy, mirin and sake marinade. The cure firms the whites and turns the yolks jammy for ramen.

why.text: The marinade pulls moisture out of the egg, which firms the white and thickens the yolk to a jam.
why.title: Salt and sugar do the curing

why.text: It lets the air pocket escape, so the egg keeps its shape and peels cleanly.
why.title: Prick the base

chefNotes.text: Heat the claypot on the stove while the sauce reduces, then tip everything in with the basil and put the lid on for 30 seconds. It arrives sizzling, the way Taiwanese restaurants serve it.
chefNotes.title: Finish in the clay pot

chefNotes.text: 800 g of bone-in thigh cut into chunks holds up better than wings in a 20-minute braise, staying juicy at 80–85 °C.
chefNotes.title: Use thighs

chefNotes.text: The reduction turns from glossy to burnt in about 30 seconds, so keep stirring and pull it the moment the sauce coats the chicken.
chefNotes.title: Watch the sugar

chefNotes.text: It gives the deep, roasted aroma behind the dish's name. Add an extra teaspoon off the heat, as heat dulls its aroma.
chefNotes.title: Use Taiwanese black sesame oil

name: Three Cup Chicken
pairing: A cold Taiwan Beer or lager, or an off-dry Riesling.

photo.alt: Glossy three cup chicken in a clay pot topped with fresh basil leaves

region: Taiwanese · San Bei Ji 三杯鸡
serveWith: Steamed jasmine rice and stir-fried greens.
source: Converted from The Woks of Life · my version: clay pot, basil on top

sourceLinks.label: Three Cup Chicken · thewoksoflife.com

steps.body:
Put the sesame oil, vegetable oil, ginger, garlic and chilli in the wok over medium heat.
Let the aromatics sizzle gently until fragrant, without browning the garlic.
Lift out the garlic and set it aside so it doesn't burn during the sear.
steps.title: Infuse the oil

steps.body:
Turn the heat to high and add the wings in one layer.
Sear until golden brown on both sides; pat them dry first so they brown instead of steaming.
steps.title: Sear the wings

steps.body: Add the warm water, Shaoxing wine, dark soy, light soy and sugar, and stir. Return the garlic.
steps.title: Add the sauce

steps.body:
Cover, turn the heat down to medium and simmer 15 minutes, or 20 for more tender meat.
The wings should reach 80 °C at the thickest part, where wing collagen turns tender.
steps.title: Covered simmer

steps.body: Uncover, turn the heat to high and reduce, stirring constantly so the sugar doesn't burn, until the sauce clings to the chicken dark and glossy.
steps.title: Reduce to a glaze

steps.body: Toss in the basil or scallions and stir-fry about 1 minute, until just wilted. Serve right away.
steps.title: Finish with basil

summary: Chicken is seared in sesame oil with ginger, garlic and chilli, then reduced with Shaoxing and soy to a dark, sticky glaze. Basil goes in at the end.

why.text: Sesame oil, rice wine and soy reduce together into a sticky, savoury glaze.
why.title: The three cups

why.text: Thai basil's anise notes are volatile, so it's tossed in just before serving.
why.title: Basil at the end

chefNotes.text: Toast the star anise, cinnamon, fennel and Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 2 minutes before bagging them. Whole spices release more aroma once heated.
chefNotes.title: Toast the spice bag

chefNotes.text: Add 3 dried shiitake to the braise. Their nucleotides multiply the glutamate already coming from the tomato, soy and bean pastes.
chefNotes.title: Add dried shiitake

chefNotes.text: Rest the beef in the broth overnight. It reabsorbs liquid, the fat sets for easy lifting, and the broth keeps 3–4 days chilled. Reheat to a boil.
chefNotes.title: Make it a day ahead

chefNotes.text: Springy yellow alkaline noodles are the classic. Fresh Shanghai or knife-cut noodles from T&T hold up better in the broth than thin white wheat noodles.
chefNotes.title: Alkaline noodles hold up in the broth

name: Taiwanese Beef Noodle Soup
pairing: A crisp lager, or an off-dry Riesling against the chili.

photo.alt: Bowl of Taiwanese beef noodle soup with sliced braised shank, bok choy, noodles, pickled mustard greens and cilantro

serveWith: Extra pickled mustard greens and chilli oil on the table.
source: Converted from Richard Ho (Ho Foods, NYC) · Munchies

sourceLinks.label: How To Make Taiwanese Beef Noodle Soup (video) · Munchies on youtube.com

steps.body: Put all the spices in cheesecloth and tie it tightly with butcher's twine. Set aside.
steps.title: Make the spice bag

steps.body:
Bring a large pot of water to a boil.
Add the beef shank and boil 2–3 minutes, until the scum rises.
Move the beef to a tray. Discard the water and wipe the pot clean.
steps.title: Blanch the beef

steps.body:
Heat the canola oil in the pot over medium-high heat.
Add the ginger, garlic and scallions and cook until fragrant, 3–4 minutes.
Add all three bean pastes and cook 2 minutes, until the oil turns red.
steps.title: Fry the aromatics and pastes

steps.body:
Stir in the rice wine and both soy sauces and cook 3 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, carrot, apple, rock sugar, onion and 3 litres of water, enough to cover the beef by 2 cm.
Return the beef to the pot and add the spice bag.
steps.title: Build the braise

steps.body:
Bring to a simmer, then hold it at a bare tremble (85–90 °C) for about 2½ hours.
It's done when a fork slides into the shank with no resistance.
steps.title: Braise the beef

steps.body:
Turn off the heat and let the beef rest in the braise so it reabsorbs liquid.
Once cooled, lift out the beef, strain the braising liquid and skim the fat. Keep both.
Taste the broth. It should be slightly over-seasoned, because the noodles dilute it.
steps.title: Rest, strain and season

steps.body:
Cut the beef against the grain into slices about 1 cm thick.
Cover and refrigerate if not serving right away. Keep the broth hot.
steps.title: Slice the beef

steps.body:
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Add the garlic and chilies and cook about 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the mustard greens and sugar and cook 1–2 minutes.
Season with salt and transfer to a bowl.
steps.title: Make the mustard greens

steps.body:
Bring a separate pot of unsalted water to a boil.
Cook the noodles according to the package, blanching the bok choy for the last minute.
Rinse the noodles under cold water, then dip them back into the boiling water just before serving.
steps.title: Cook the noodles

steps.body:
Season each bowl:
- 1 tsp light soy
- 1 tsp sesame oil
- ½ tsp black vinegar
- A pinch of white pepper
Add the noodles and ladle over the hot broth.
Top with sliced beef and bok choy, then garnish with scallions, cilantro and mustard greens.
steps.title: Assemble the bowl

summary: Beef shank braises for two and a half hours in a bean-paste and soy broth with a bag of toasted spices. It's served over wheat noodles with pickled mustard greens, bok choy and cilantro.

why.text: A quick boil clears blood and scum, so the braise stays clean.
why.title: Blanch first

why.text: Frying in oil deepens their flavour and turns the oil red, which colours the broth.
why.title: Fry the bean pastes

chefNotes.text: Capsaicin dissolves into alcohol, so a strained infusion gives the same heat in every glass, which muddling doesn't.
chefNotes.title: Infuse the bottle, don't muddle each drink

chefNotes.text: Fresh juice is brighter, and juice a few hours old is fine. Bottled lime is what makes margaritas taste flat.
chefNotes.title: Squeeze the lime the same day

chefNotes.text: Mix the salt 2:1 with Tajín to bring heat to the first sip.
chefNotes.title: A Tajín rim adds heat to the first sip

chefNotes.text: 60 ml jalapeño-infused agave syrup and water (1:1), 30 ml lime and 60 ml soda, served over ice with the same rim.
chefNotes.title: Infused agave keeps the zero-proof spicy

items.name: Jalapeños

name: Spicy Margarita
pairing: It's the drink, so serve it with salty, spicy food.

photo.alt: Spicy margarita on the rocks in a polka-dot glass with a salt rim and jalapeño slices

restNote: one-time jalapeño infusion for the bottle
serveWith: Cumin lamb chops, tacos al pastor, or anything off the grill.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Spicy Margarita · diffordsguide.com

steps.body:
Drop the sliced jalapeños into the bottle of tequila.
Taste every 5 minutes and strain once it's as hot as you like; seeded slices are usually ready in 15–20 minutes.
steps.title: Infuse the tequila

steps.body:
Run the lime wedge around the outer rim of a rocks glass and roll it in salt. Keep the salt on the outside so it doesn't fall into the drink.
Fill the glass with fresh ice.
steps.title: Rim the glass

steps.body:
Add the infused tequila, Cointreau, lime and agave to a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds, which reaches full chill and dilution.
steps.title: Shake hard

steps.body: Strain over the fresh ice and float two thin jalapeño rounds on top. They signal the heat and keep infusing as you drink.
steps.title: Strain and garnish

summary: The heat comes from jalapeño-infused blanco tequila, shaken hard with fresh lime, Cointreau and agave. It's served over ice in a salt-rimmed rocks glass.

why.text: Capsaicin dissolves in alcohol, so a quick infusion makes the heat consistent from glass to glass.
why.title: Infuse the spirit, not the drink

chefNotes.text: Squid and cuttlefish are tender only if flashed or braised long, with nothing good in between. Flash them at the very end, and give the octopus its long simmer separately beforehand.
chefNotes.title: Squid: 90 seconds or 30 minutes

chefNotes.text: The clam and mussel juices are the sauce's umami backbone, adding nucleotides to the tomato's glutamate. Never pour them off, and go easy on the salt.
chefNotes.title: The shellfish liquor is the stock

chefNotes.text: The sauce is already salty from the shellfish, so the pasta needs only light seasoning.
chefNotes.title: Season the pasta water at about 7 g per litre

chefNotes.text: It cooks for minutes, not an hour, which is why the sauce is lighter and fresher than a slow ragù.
chefNotes.title: Blended raw tomato stays bright

items.note: ripe, or 1 can whole plum; blended smooth

items.name: Kosher salt

name: Seafood Spaghetti Allo Scoglio
pairing: New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, such as Oyster Bay, or a crisp Vermentino.

photo.alt: Seafood spaghetti with half a lobster, clams, mussels, squid and blistered cherry tomatoes

serveWith: Crusty bread for the sauce, and a green salad.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Spaghetti allo Scoglio · giallozafferano.com

steps.body:
If the octopus is raw, simmer it gently in unsalted water until a knife slides into the thickest part.
Cool and cut into pieces. Skip this step if it's pre-cooked.
steps.title: Tenderise the octopus

steps.body:
Soak the clams in salted cold water for 30 minutes so they spit out their grit.
Blend the tomatoes until smooth.
Plunge the lobster into boiling water for 2 minutes, then split it lengthwise and crack the claws.
steps.title: Purge and prep

steps.body:
In a wide pan, warm the olive oil with the garlic and chilli until the garlic just turns pale gold.
Add the cherry tomatoes and cook until they blister and start to burst.
steps.title: Garlic and cherry tomatoes

steps.body:
Add the wine, clams and mussels, cover and cook until they open.
Lift them out as they open and discard any that stay shut. Keep the juices in the pan.
steps.title: Steam open the shellfish

steps.body:
Pour in the blended tomato and simmer to reduce slightly.
Nestle the lobster in, flesh side down, until its meat is opaque.
steps.title: Build the sauce

steps.body: Boil 4 litres of water with the salt and cook the spaghetti while the sauce reduces, 2 minutes short of the packet time; it finishes in the sauce.
steps.title: Cook the pasta

steps.body: Add the squid, cuttlefish and octopus and cook just until the squid turns opaque. Any longer and it goes rubbery.
steps.title: Flash the squid

steps.body:
Toss the spaghetti in with a ladle of pasta water until the sauce clings and turns glossy.
Return the clams and mussels, then finish with parsley, lemon zest and a drizzle of olive oil.
steps.title: Finish the pasta in the sauce

summary: The sauce is blended fresh tomato and the shellfish's own juices, tossed with spaghetti, half a lobster, clams, mussels, squid, cuttlefish and octopus. Blistered cherry tomatoes and parsley finish it.

why.text: Starch from the pasta and its water emulsifies the oil and shellfish juices into a sauce that clings.
why.title: Finish the pasta in the sauce

why.text: Wine steams the clams and mussels open and adds acidity. Parsley and lemon zest freshen it at the end.
why.title: Wine opens the shellfish

chefNotes.text: Coconut and pumpkin are sweet and rich, so acid does more than salt here. Add lime a little at a time.
chefNotes.title: Lime, not more salt

chefNotes.text: For a Thai lean, fry a teaspoon of red curry paste with the ginger. Its aroma is fat-soluble, so it blooms in the butter.
chefNotes.title: Bloom some curry paste

chefNotes.text: Kabocha from T&T is drier and nuttier than sugar pumpkin, so the soup comes out thicker and deeper in colour.
chefNotes.title: Kabocha for body

chefNotes.text: The soup keeps 3–4 days chilled and freezes well. Reheat gently and adjust the lime.
chefNotes.title: It keeps and freezes well

name: Pumpkin Coconut Soup
pairing: An off-dry Riesling matches the coconut and ginger.

photo.alt: Bowl of pumpkin coconut soup with a coconut milk swirl and cilantro

serveWith: Crusty bread, or a crisp green salad with a sharp vinaigrette.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Thai Coconut Pumpkin Soup · recipetineats.com

steps.body:
Heat the oven to 200 °C.
Rub the cut sides of the pumpkin with oil and salt, then roast cut side down on a sheet pan.
It's done when it's soft through and browned underneath; the browning adds depth.
steps.title: Roast the pumpkin

steps.body:
Melt the butter in a pot over medium-low heat. Cook the onion until soft and sweet but not coloured.
Add the garlic and ginger for the last minute.
steps.title: Sweat the aromatics

steps.body: Scoop the pumpkin flesh into the pot, add the chicken stock and simmer.
steps.title: Simmer

steps.body:
Add the coconut milk and blend until completely smooth and glossy.
Thin with stock if needed until it coats a spoon. Warm through, but don't boil it hard or the coconut milk can split.
steps.title: Blend with coconut milk

steps.body: Season with salt first, then lime juice, then fish sauce if it tastes flat.
steps.title: Balance

steps.body: Ladle into bowls. Swirl in coconut milk from a spoon, then add cilantro and cracked pepper.
steps.title: Garnish

summary: Roasted pumpkin is blended with chicken stock, coconut milk and ginger, and lime brightens it. A swirl of coconut milk, cilantro and cracked pepper finish the bowl.

why.text: Curry paste and ginger aromas dissolve in coconut fat, so frying them first flavours the whole pot.
why.title: Fat carries the aromatics

why.text: Acid keeps the sweet pumpkin and coconut from tasting heavy.
why.title: Lime at the end

chefNotes.text: After skimming, hold it at a lazy simmer (about 90 °C). A hard boil emulsifies the fat and clouds the broth; a gentle one keeps it clear and clean.
chefNotes.title: Simmer, don't boil

chefNotes.text: Cold water brings the proteins out slowly, so the scum rises in one go and skims off cleanly.
chefNotes.title: Start in cold water

chefNotes.text: Dill's aroma fades with long cooking. Strain out the cooked dill as written, then add a small handful of fresh chopped dill to each bowl.
chefNotes.title: Fresh dill to finish

chefNotes.text: Dried jujubes add a soft, honeyed sweetness that rounds out the salty soup base. Score or tear a few so they release more into the broth, or add 3 slices of ginger to lean further Chinese.
chefNotes.title: Red dates give it an Asian lean

pairing: A dry Riesling or a crisp lager.

serveWith: Rye bread and sour cream on the side. Make-ahead: chill overnight, lift off the set fat, then reheat to a boil.

steps.body:
Rinse the meat and vegetables.
Throughout, top up with water to keep the meat and vegetables submerged.
steps.title: Rinse

steps.body:
Put the meat in the pot with the water and bring to a boil.
Skim the foam until almost none rises.
steps.title: Bring up and skim

steps.body: Turn the heat down to a lazy simmer, a few bubbles breaking the surface, for about 1 hour. A hard boil clouds the broth.
steps.title: Cook the meat

steps.body:
Add the carrots, celery, onion, parsnip, red dates, peppercorns, chicken soup base and Vegeta.
Cook until the beef is fork-tender, 30–40 minutes or more.
steps.title: Add vegetables and seasoning

steps.body: Add the parsley and dill and cook 15 minutes more.
steps.title: Add the herbs

steps.body:
Discard the onion, celery, parsnip and herbs; keep the carrots, red dates and meat.
Taste before adding salt, since the soup base and Vegeta are both very salty.
steps.title: Strain and season

steps.body: Put cooked rice or noodles in each bowl and ladle over the broth, meat, carrots and a few red dates.
steps.title: Serve

summary: This family soup simmers beef shank or oxtail with chicken legs, root vegetables, dill and red dates. The dates add a gentle Chinese-style sweetness, and it's served over rice or noodles.

why.text: Scum rises at the first boil; a gentle simmer afterwards keeps the broth clear.
why.title: Skim, then lazy simmer

why.text: Dill's fresh, anise-like notes and parsnip's sweetness are the Eastern European signature. Red dates push that sweetness in a Chinese direction.
why.title: Dill and parsnip

chefNotes.text: Peppery heat is Nagoya's signature (Sekai no Yamachan style), so keep grinding.
chefNotes.title: More pepper than you'd think

chefNotes.text: The 160 °C pass cooks the wing and renders the fat, and the 180 °C pass crisps the skin in two minutes without overcooking.
chefNotes.title: Double-fry

chefNotes.text: 200 °C for 20–22 minutes, shaking halfway, then glaze. You get nearly the same crunch without a pot of oil.
chefNotes.title: The air fryer nearly matches the crunch

chefNotes.text: Real tebasaki is lacquered rather than saucy, so brush the glaze on hot skin and let any excess drip off.
chefNotes.title: Brush, don't drown

name: Nagoya Tebasaki Wings
pairing: An ice-cold lager or a whisky highball.

photo.alt: Glazed Nagoya tebasaki chicken wings with crushed sesame and nori on a blossom-patterned plate

steps.body:
Pat the wings dry, season with salt and dust lightly with potato starch.
A thin coat crisps better than a thick batter.
steps.title: Dry and dust

steps.body:
Simmer the soy, mirin, sake, sugar, garlic and ginger until syrupy and reduced by about a third.
Keep it warm.
steps.title: Make the glaze

steps.body:
Heat the oil to 160 °C.
Fry the wings in batches until pale golden and cooked through (80 °C at the thickest part), then rest them on a rack.
steps.title: First fry

steps.body:
Raise the oil to 180 °C and fry again until deep golden and crackly.
The second fry drives off the surface moisture the first left behind.
steps.title: Second fry

steps.body:
Brush the hot wings with the glaze so the crust stays crisp, then shower them with black pepper, sesame and crumbled nori.
Serve right away.
steps.title: Glaze and season

summary: Nagoya's izakaya wings are double-fried until crackly, then lacquered in a sweet soy-mirin glaze. Black pepper, crushed sesame and nori finish them.

why.text: Brushing glaze on keeps the double-fried crust crisp.
why.title: Brush, don't toss

why.text: Plenty of black pepper is the Nagoya signature, sharp heat against a sticky, sweet glaze.
why.title: Pepper against sweet soy

chefNotes.text: The spices' aroma is fat-soluble, so a full minute in the butter brings out far more than stirring them into stock.
chefNotes.title: Bloom the curry powder in the roux

chefNotes.text: The beef stock supplies nucleotides, and a teaspoon of instant dashi or 1 tbsp of tonkatsu sauce adds glutamate. Together they give the curry the depth of a shop-bought roux.
chefNotes.title: Add one more umami source

chefNotes.text: Japanese curry is famously better on day two, once the starch sets and the flavours meld. Thin it with a splash of water when you reheat.
chefNotes.title: Make it a day ahead

chefNotes.text: The Le Creuset braiser handles the sauce stage and the reheat well, but the 2-litre beef simmer needs a taller pot.
chefNotes.title: Simmer the beef in a taller pot

name: Japanese Beef Curry
pairing: A Japanese lager, or an off-dry Riesling to balance the sweet-spicy sauce.

photo.alt: Japanese beef curry with carrots, potatoes and mushrooms beside white rice and yellow takuan pickles

steps.body:
Season the beef with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef well in batches; don't crowd the pot.
steps.title: Brown the beef

steps.body:
Return all the beef to the pot, add the water to cover and bring to a simmer.
Simmer 1–1½ hours, skimming off any scum, until the beef is tender but not falling apart.
steps.title: Simmer the beef

steps.body:
Add the carrots and potatoes and simmer about 15 minutes, until tender.
Strain, keeping the solids and the stock separately.
steps.title: Cook the vegetables

steps.body:
In a second large pot, melt the butter and cook the onion over medium heat until soft and golden, about 10 minutes. Add the flour and cook, stirring, until the roux just starts to colour.
Stir in the curry powder (and garam masala, if using) and chilli powder for 1 minute.
steps.title: Make the roux

steps.body:
Add the stock a ladle at a time, stirring, until you have a smooth sauce.
Add more stock or water if it's too thick.
steps.title: Build the sauce

steps.body:
Add the mushrooms, grated apple, ketchup, Worcestershire, soy sauce and salt.
Simmer about 10 minutes, stirring often so it doesn't catch, until the mushrooms are soft.
steps.title: Simmer the aromatics

steps.body:
Off the heat, stir in the beef, potatoes and carrots.
Cover and let stand at least 15 minutes so the flavours settle.
steps.title: Combine and rest

steps.body:
Taste and adjust the salt (it usually needs more).
Serve with rice and pickles.
steps.title: Season and serve

summary: Beef chuck simmers until tender, then folds into a from-scratch curry roux with apple, onion, mushrooms, ketchup and Worcestershire. It's served with rice and Japanese pickles.

why.text: Apple adds a soft sweetness and helps thicken the sauce, rounding off the spice.

why.text: Curry powder's aroma dissolves in fat, so a minute in butter beats stirring it into stock.
why.title: Bloom the curry in the roux

chefNotes.text: A flattened bird roasts in about 80 minutes at 220 °C, and the breast and thighs finish together instead of the breast drying out while the legs catch up. Roast the backbone with the vegetables for a richer gravy.

chefNotes.text: It raises the skin's pH and draws out moisture, so it browns faster and crackles.
chefNotes.title: Baking powder gives crisper skin

chefNotes.text: A teaspoon adds glutamate to the turkey's nucleotides, so the gravy tastes deeper without tasting of soy.
chefNotes.title: Soy in the gravy

chefNotes.text: Roast 1 kg of turkey wings 2 days ahead and make the gravy base with them. On the day, whisk in the pan juices.

name: Herb-Butter Roast Turkey with Dijon Pan Gravy
pairing: An Ontario Pinot Noir or a lightly oaked Chardonnay. Both are high-acid, so they handle the gravy.

photo.alt: Sliced roast turkey breast with pale Dijon gravy beside a bowl of pumpkin soup

serveWith: Pumpkin coconut soup, roast beets or purple sweet potato, cranberry sauce.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Easy Herb-Roasted Turkey with Gravy · americastestkitchen.com

steps.body:
Pat the turkey dry. Mix the salt, baking powder and pepper and rub it all over, including inside the cavity.
Refrigerate uncovered on a rack for 24–48 hours so the skin dries out.
steps.title: Dry-brine the bird

steps.body: Mash the butter with the sage, thyme, rosemary, garlic and lemon zest.
steps.title: Make the herb butter

steps.body:
Loosen the breast and thigh skin with your fingers and spread most of the herb butter underneath. Rub the rest on the outside.
Put the lemon halves in the cavity. Leave the bird out for 1 hour to take the chill off.
steps.title: Butter under the skin

steps.body:
Heat the oven to 220 °C.
Scatter the onion, carrot and celery in the roasting pan, pour in the stock and set the turkey on top.
Roast until the skin starts to colour.
steps.title: Hot start

steps.body:
Drop the oven to 165 °C and roast until the thickest part of the breast reads 74 °C and the thigh reads 82 °C, about 2 hours for 5.5 kg.
Start checking at 90 minutes. If the breast is running ahead, tent it with foil.
steps.title: Roast low to temperature

steps.body:
Move the turkey to a board and tent it loosely with foil.
Rest 30–45 minutes; the juices settle and carving stays clean.
steps.title: Rest

steps.body:
Set the roasting pan over medium heat, add the wine and scrape up the browned bits for 2 minutes.
Strain everything into a fat separator, pressing on the vegetables. Spoon off 60 g of fat for the roux.
steps.title: Deglaze and separate

steps.body: In a saucepan over medium heat, cook the fat and flour, whisking, until it smells nutty and turns pale gold.
steps.title: Make a blond roux

steps.body:
Whisk in the warm stock gradually, then the defatted pan juices.
Simmer, whisking, until it coats a spoon.
Finish with the Dijon and soy, then season with salt and pepper.
steps.title: Build the gravy

steps.body:
Take off the breasts whole and slice them across the grain about 1.5 cm thick.
Separate the thighs and drumsticks. Spoon gravy over just before serving.
steps.title: Carve

summary: A dry-brined turkey roasts with sage, thyme and rosemary butter under the skin. A pale gravy built on a blond roux and finished with Dijon goes alongside.

why.text: It bastes the breast from the inside and carries the herbs, while the skin on top still crisps.
why.title: Butter under the skin

why.text: Mustard helps bind the fat into the stock, and its acid lightens a rich gravy.
why.title: Dijon in the gravy

chefNotes.text: Keep the seeds and membranes in one red chilli. That's where the capsaicin is, and it carries into the wine and fat.
chefNotes.title: Keep the membranes for more heat

chefNotes.text: Scrape off the wet marinade or the shanks steam at 100 °C instead of browning.
chefNotes.title: Dry before searing

chefNotes.text: Reduce the strained sauce on the stove and swirl in 20 g of cold butter off the heat.
chefNotes.title: Cold butter makes it glossy

chefNotes.text: Braise the day before and chill it in the pot. The fat sets for easy lifting, and the meat reheats gently at 160 °C covered.
chefNotes.title: Braise the day before

name: Gordon Ramsay's Fiery Lamb Shanks
pairing: Syrah or Nebbiolo is the classic match. A New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc also works, since its acidity and herbal edge pick up the mint and chilli.

photo.alt: Braised lamb shank over mashed potato with red wine sauce, mint and scallions

serveWith: Buttery mash, with green beans or roasted carrots.

sourceLinks.label: Slow-Cooked Fiery Lamb · gordonramsay.com

steps.body:
Mix the chillies, paprika, oregano, cumin, cinnamon, garlic, olive oil, salt and pepper.
Rub it into the shanks and marinate for 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.
steps.title: Marinate the shanks

steps.body:
Heat the oven to 160 °C.
Scrape the marinade off the shanks and keep it, then pat the meat dry.
steps.title: Heat the oven

steps.body:
Heat the oil in a heavy ovenproof pot over medium-high heat and brown the shanks on all sides until deep brown.
Add the reserved chillies and cinnamon for the last minute, then lift everything out.
steps.title: Sear the lamb

steps.body:
Add the carrots, onion and bay leaves and fry until lightly coloured.
Set the shanks back on top.
steps.title: Colour the vegetables

steps.body: Pour in the wine, scrape up the browned bits and boil hard until reduced by half.
steps.title: Reduce the wine

steps.body:
Add the stock and bring back to a boil.
Move the pot to the oven, uncovered, and braise until the meat is almost falling off the bone and the sauce is glossy.
Turn and baste the shanks every 45 minutes so the tops don't dry out.
steps.title: Braise uncovered

steps.body:
In the last 40 minutes, simmer the potatoes in salted water until a knife slides through.
Drain and let them steam-dry for 2 minutes.
Rice or mash with the butter, then beat in the warm milk and season.
steps.title: Make the mash

steps.body:
Lift out the shanks. Skim the fat from the sauce and pick out the bay and cinnamon.
If the sauce is thin, boil it on the stove until it coats a spoon.
steps.title: Finish the sauce

steps.body:
Spoon the mash into shallow bowls, set a shank on top and ladle over the sauce.
Finish with torn mint and scallions.
steps.title: Plate

summary: Lamb shanks are rubbed with chilli, smoked paprika, cumin, oregano and cinnamon, then braised uncovered in a bottle of red wine until the meat falls off the bone. They're served over buttery mash with torn mint.

why.text: Alcohol and acid lift the browned bits from the pan into the braise, and that's where the deep flavour comes from.
why.title: Wine dissolves the fond

why.text: Heat cuts through lamb's richness, the same reason mint and cumin pair with it.
why.title: Chilli with lamb

chefNotes.text: Shoyu tare in a chintan-style double soup is classic Tokyo. The soup gives body and the tare gives the bowl its character, so season the bowl, never the pot. 25–35 ml is the range.
chefNotes.title: Tare names the bowl

chefNotes.text: The kombu and shiitake bring glutamate, the niboshi and dried prawns bring nucleotides, and the pork bones add more. That combination is why a double soup tastes far deeper than either half.
chefNotes.title: Stacked umami gives the depth

chefNotes.text: The meat soup stays clear (chintan) only if it never rolls; a hard boil emulsifies the fat and clouds it.
chefNotes.title: Keep it below a boil

chefNotes.text: Duck fat and lard carry aroma better than neutral oil, but keep the oil under 130 °C or the garlic turns bitter.
chefNotes.title: Fat stays fragrant

name: Double Soup Shoyu Ramen
pairing: A cold Japanese lager or a dry junmai sake.

photo.alt: Shoyu ramen with rolled chashu, marinated eggs, braised shiitake, nori and scallions

region: Tokyo-style shoyu · Adam Liaw's Ramen School
restNote: eggs cure 48 h; chashu chills overnight
serveWith: Gyoza or karaage on the side. The soup freezes for 3 months; the eggs keep 4 days in the marinade.
source: Converted from Adam Liaw's Ramen School · aroma oil and tare are my own

sourceLinks.label: Ramen School 006: Rich Double Soup · adamliaw.com
Ramen School 002: Three Styles of Chashu · adamliaw.com
Ramen School 003: Ajitama (Ramen Eggs) · adamliaw.com

steps.body:
Cover the rolled belly with cold water, bring to a boil and simmer 20 minutes.
Rinse the pork and scrub out the pot to get rid of the scum.
steps.title: Day 1: blanch the chashu

steps.body:
Return the pork with the kombu and shiitake, cover with water and bring up.
Pull the kombu as the water starts to steam.
Add the salt and sugar, then simmer under a drop lid for 1 hour.
steps.title: Braise the chashu, part one

steps.body:
Add both soy sauces, the mirin, the sake and 1 l of water, and simmer another hour, until a skewer slides in easily.
Chill the pork overnight in the liquid. Keep the liquid (it becomes the tare and the egg cure) and the shiitake.
Strain the liquid and reduce it to about 600 ml; this is the tare.
steps.title: Braise the chashu, part two

steps.body:
Prick the base of each egg, lower into simmering water and cook 6 minutes, then ice them.
Peel, and submerge in 250 ml of cooled chashu liquid plus 500 ml of water.
Refrigerate 48 hours.
steps.title: Boil and cure the eggs

steps.body:
Put the chicken frames, pork bones, chicken feet and trotters in 8 l of water and bring to a simmer.
Skim hard for 75 minutes, uncovered.
steps.title: Day 2: meat soup

steps.body:
Add the onions, carrots and shiitake and simmer gently about 5 hours more, never boiling.
Strain, pressing the bones.
steps.title: Add the vegetables

steps.body:
Soak the kombu in 3 l of cold water in the fridge for 1 hour.
Heat slowly over about an hour and pull the kombu just before it boils.
Add the fish maw, prawns and niboshi and simmer 45 minutes, then strain.
steps.title: Gyokai soup

steps.body:
Combine both soups and reduce by a third.
Chill, then lift off the set fat and add it to the aroma oil.
steps.title: Combine and reduce

steps.body:
Warm the duck fat and lard over medium-low heat with the scallion greens, garlic, ginger and shallot.
Fry gently until the aromatics are golden but not dark, about 120 °C, then strain.
steps.title: Aroma oil

steps.body:
Into each hot bowl, put 30 ml tare (taste, and go up to 40–45 ml) and 1 tbsp aroma oil, then 400 ml boiling soup.
Cook the noodles, drain hard and add them to the bowl.
steps.title: Day 3: build the bowls

steps.body:
Sear thick slices of chashu with a torch or in a hot pan, and halve the eggs.
Top each bowl with chashu, the egg, braised shiitake, nori and scallions.
steps.title: Top

summary: This shoyu ramen layers a pork-and-chicken bone soup with a kombu, niboshi and dried-prawn gyokai stock. The chashu braise becomes the tare, duck fat and lard make the aroma oil, and rolled chashu, 48-hour ajitama, shiitake and nori top the bowl.

why.text: The meat soup brings body and glutamate, and the seafood soup brings nucleotides. Together they taste far stronger than either.
why.title: Two soups multiply umami

why.text: The broth is left unseasoned so the tare sets the salt in each bowl.
why.title: Tare carries the salt

chefNotes.text: Cumin's aroma compounds release with heat, and leaving some seeds whole gives a crunchy crust.
chefNotes.title: Toast, then crack

chefNotes.text: Wet marinade steams at 100 °C, and the honey scorches before it browns. A drier surface gets real Maillard crust in 2–3 minutes.
chefNotes.title: Wipe before grilling

chefNotes.text: 200 °C for 8–10 minutes, flipping halfway. You lose the grill marks but keep the crust.
chefNotes.title: The air fryer keeps the crust

chefNotes.text: Health Canada's minimum for lamb is 63 °C. Chef medium-rare (52–54 °C) is fine for intact chops, but use 63 °C for vulnerable guests.
chefNotes.title: Use 63 °C for vulnerable guests

name: Cumin Lamb Chops
pairing: A cold lager, or a juicy Grenache or Syrah.

photo.alt: Grilled cumin lamb chops with chilli flakes, cilantro and scallions on a white plate

serveWith: Cucumber smashed with black vinegar and garlic, and steamed rice or flatbread.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Grilled Lamb Chops · thewoksoflife.com

steps.body:
Toast the cumin and Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan until fragrant and a shade darker.
Crush coarsely in a mortar, leaving plenty of whole cumin seeds for texture.
Set a third aside for finishing.
steps.title: Toast and crack the spices

steps.body:
Mix the remaining spices with the chilli flakes, soy, Shaoxing, oyster sauce, honey, garlic, ginger and oil.
Coat the chops and marinate 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.
steps.title: Marinate

steps.body:
Leave the chops at room temperature for 20 minutes so they cook evenly to the bone.
Wipe off excess marinade; the honey burns before the meat cooks.
steps.title: Take the chill off

steps.body:
Heat a cast-iron grill pan until smoking and brush it with oil.
Grill the chops 2–3 minutes per side, turning once for clean marks.
Pull at 52–54 °C for medium-rare or 57 °C for medium.
steps.title: Grill hot

steps.body: Mix the glaze and brush it over the hot chops. Rest 5 minutes.
steps.title: Glaze and rest

steps.body: Scatter over the reserved cumin, cilantro and scallions. Serve straight away.
steps.title: Finish

summary: Frenched lamb chops are marinated in toasted cumin, Sichuan pepper, chilli, soy and garlic, then grilled hot. A chilli-oil glaze, more cumin, cilantro and scallion finish them.

why.text: Cumin's earthy, warm notes stand up to lamb's strong flavour. It's the Xinjiang pairing.
why.title: Cumin with lamb

why.text: Heat releases cumin's aroma oils; whole seeds left in add crunch.
why.title: Toast before grinding

chefNotes.text: Lay the crawfish tails down before the lettuce so they show through the wrapper.
chefNotes.title: Protein first, against the paper

chefNotes.text: 2–3 seconds is enough, since it keeps softening as you fill it. A fully floppy sheet tears.
chefNotes.title: Under-soak the rice paper

chefNotes.text: Toss the peeled tails with 1 tsp fish sauce and a squeeze of lime before rolling. Plain boiled crawfish taste flat once wrapped in noodles and lettuce.
chefNotes.title: Season the tails

chefNotes.text: Cover the rolls with a damp towel. They hold for up to 2 hours at room temperature; don't refrigerate, as the paper goes hard.
chefNotes.title: Hold under a damp towel, never chilled

name: Crawfish Summer Rolls
pairing: A dry Riesling, Grüner Veltliner or a crisp lager.

photo.alt: Crawfish summer rolls in rice paper with whole boiled crawfish on a dark plate

serveWith: The whole crawfish for picking, and a light soup.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Vietnamese Spring Rolls (Goi Cuon) · hungryhuy.com

steps.body:
Bring a big pot of water to a rolling boil with the salt, lemon and garlic.
Add the crawfish, return to the boil and cook 3 minutes, then turn off the heat and let them soak 15 minutes for flavour.
Shells should be bright red and the tail meat opaque.
steps.title: Boil the crawfish

steps.body:
Keep a few whole crawfish for the plate.
Twist off the tails, peel them, and halve any large ones lengthwise so they lie flat against the paper.
steps.title: Peel the tails

steps.body: Cook the vermicelli in boiling water, then rinse cold and drain well; wet noodles tear the paper.
steps.title: Cook the vermicelli

steps.body:
Whisk the hoisin, peanut butter, warm water, lime, garlic and sriracha until smooth.
Top with crushed peanuts.
steps.title: Make the dip

steps.body:
Dip the rice paper one sheet at a time in warm water for 2–3 seconds; it finishes softening on the board.
Lay 3 tail halves cut side down along the bottom third, then lettuce, noodles, cucumber and herbs.
Fold in the sides and roll up tightly.
steps.title: Roll

steps.body: Cut on the diagonal and serve right away with the dip and whole crawfish on the side.
steps.title: Serve

summary: Rice-paper rolls are packed with boiled crawfish tails, butter lettuce, vermicelli, cucumber and fresh herbs. They're served with a peanut-hoisin dip and whole crawfish on the side.

why.text: It keeps absorbing water from the fillings, so a firm sheet softens to the right texture on the board.
why.title: Under-soak the rice paper

why.text: Mint and cilantro add a fresh lift against the rich peanut-hoisin sauce.
why.title: Herbs against the dip

chefNotes.text: The liquid that collects on the plate carries the muddy, fishy flavour. Pouring it off and adding fresh sauce is what makes the restaurant version taste clean.
chefNotes.title: Discard the steaming juices

chefNotes.text: The ginger-scallion raft or a pair of chopsticks lets steam circulate underneath, so both sides cook evenly.
chefNotes.title: Raise the fish off the plate

chefNotes.text: Around 200 °C, it blooms the raw ginger and scallion in a second and releases their aroma. Lukewarm oil just makes them greasy.
chefNotes.title: The hot oil does the cooking

chefNotes.text: Restaurants pull at the point of just flaking (about 60 °C) for silky flesh. Health Canada's minimum for fish is 70 °C, so use that for vulnerable guests.
chefNotes.title: Pull at just-flaking, about 60 °C

name: Cantonese Steamed Fish
pairing: A dry Riesling or an unoaked Chablis.

photo.alt: Whole Cantonese steamed sea bass in soy dressing with julienned scallion and cilantro

serveWith: Steamed jasmine rice spooned with the soy sauce, and gai lan with oyster sauce.

sourceLinks.label: Closest published recipe: Cantonese Steamed Fish · thewoksoflife.com

steps.body:
Pat the fish dry and score it on both sides down to the bone, about 2 cm apart.
Lay the sliced ginger and scallion lengths on a heatproof plate as a raft, set the fish on top and stuff a few slices into the cavity.
Splash with Shaoxing.
steps.title: Score and line

steps.body:
Steam over a full rolling boil, covered, until the flesh at the thickest point flakes from the backbone and the eyes turn white.
Allow about 8 minutes per 2.5 cm of thickness.
steps.title: Steam hard

steps.body:
Lift out the plate, discard the cooked ginger and scallion and tip away the fishy steaming liquid.
Move the fish to a clean platter.
steps.title: Pour off the liquid

steps.body:
Warm the soy, hot water and sugar until the sugar dissolves, then pour it around the fish, not over the skin.
Pile the julienned ginger and scallion along the top.
steps.title: Dress

steps.body:
Heat the oil until just smoking, about 200 °C, and pour it over the aromatics so they crackle.
Scatter the cilantro and serve at once.
steps.title: Sizzle the oil

summary: A whole scored sea bass steams over a ginger-scallion raft, then gets a light soy dressing. Smoking oil poured over julienned ginger, scallion and cilantro finishes it at the table.

why.text: It carries the cloudy, fishy proteins the fish gives off, so fresh soy sauce goes on instead.
why.title: Pour off the steaming liquid

why.text: Smoking-hot oil flash-cooks the raw ginger and scallion, releasing their aroma straight into the sauce.
why.title: Sizzling oil finishes it

chefNotes.text: Steam trapped under the cutlet softens the bottom crust within a minute, so give the air somewhere to go.
chefNotes.title: Rest on a rack

chefNotes.text: Cooler oil soaks into the panko, and hotter oil browns it before the centre is done. Fry two at a time so the temperature doesn't drop.
chefNotes.title: Hold the oil at 170 °C

chefNotes.text: Spray the breaded chops well with oil and cook at 200 °C for 12–14 minutes, flipping halfway. They come out a little less puffy but still crisp.
chefNotes.title: The air fryer gets close

chefNotes.text: 63 °C with a rest is juicy with a blush of pink, which is the USDA standard. Health Canada says 71 °C for chops, so use that for vulnerable guests.
chefNotes.title: 63 °C with a rest stays juicy

name: Adam Liaw's Tonkatsu
pairing: A cold Japanese lager, or a dry Riesling to cut the fat.

photo.alt: Sliced pork tonkatsu with red sauce, rice, wakame salad, cucumber and tomato wedges

serveWith: Rice, shredded cabbage, miso soup and pickles; in my version, wakame salad, cucumber and tomato with a sweet chilli sauce. Leftovers make katsu kare with the Japanese Beef Curry sauce.

sourceLinks.label: How to Make Tonkatsu · adamliaw.com

steps.body:
Pat the chops dry.
Snip the fat edge of each chop in 3–4 places so it doesn't curl, then season with salt.
steps.title: Prep the pork

steps.body:
Set out the flour, egg and panko in three trays.
Dredge each chop in flour and tap off the excess, dip it in egg, then press it firmly into the panko.
Rest on a rack while the oil heats so the coating sets.
steps.title: Bread

steps.body: Heat the oil in a heavy pot to 170 °C; panko sizzles steadily the moment it hits the oil.
steps.title: Heat the oil

steps.body:
Fry two at a time, turning once, until deep golden.
Take the cutlets out as soon as the oil turns lively and spits; that's the meat releasing its juice, Liaw's cue that it's done.
Probe for 60–63 °C in the centre.
steps.title: Fry

steps.body:
Stand the cutlets upright on a rack, not paper, so steam escapes and the bottom stays crisp.
Carryover takes the centre to about 63 °C.
steps.title: Rest on a rack

steps.body: Mix the ketchup, Worcestershire, soy and mustard.
steps.title: Make the sauce

steps.body:
Slice into 2 cm strips.
Serve with rice, shredded cabbage, cucumber, tomato, lemon, pickles and the sauce.
steps.title: Slice and serve

summary: Thick pork loin chops are breaded in flour, egg and panko and deep-fried at 170 °C until golden. They're served with rice, cucumber, tomato and a quick ketchup-Worcestershire tonkatsu sauce.

why.text: Flour dries the surface so the egg sticks, and the egg glues on the panko. Panko's big flakes soak up less oil, so they stay crisp.
why.title: Flour, egg, panko

why.text: On a rack, steam escapes from all sides, so the bottom crust doesn't go soggy.
why.title: Rest it standing up

chefNotes.text: A dry surface browns at 140–165 °C instead of steaming at 100 °C, and the dark soy's sugars lacquer it.
chefNotes.title: The overnight dry is what makes the skin crack

chefNotes.text: The garlic and chilli mellow after 20 minutes in the vinegar, so make it while the bird roasts.
chefNotes.title: Make the sauce first

chefNotes.text: Flattened, the bird roasts evenly in about 45 minutes at 220 °C, and more of the skin faces the heat.
chefNotes.title: Spatchcock to roast in 45 minutes

chefNotes.text: The chicken fat is what rounds off the vinegar's edge. Don't skip it, and add more if the sauce tastes sharp.
chefNotes.title: Use the drippings

items.name: Cilantro
items.note: root and stalks finely chopped; leaves kept

name: Adam Liaw's Shandong Roast Chicken
pairing: An off-dry Riesling matches the vinegar and chilli; a crisp lager also works.

photo.alt: Carved Shandong roast chicken with lacquered skin under a garlic, chilli and cilantro vinegar sauce

serveWith: Steamed rice and smashed cucumber or stir-fried greens.

sourceLinks.label: Shandong Roast Chicken · adamliaw.com

steps.body:
Salt the chicken inside and out, rubbing off any loose skin.
Set it on a rack in the sink and pour boiling water over the skin until it tightens.
steps.title: Salt and scald

steps.body:
Rub the skin with the dark soy, Shaoxing and ginger juice.
Refrigerate uncovered overnight so the skin dries to a parchment-like finish.
Short on time? A hairdryer on cool works.
steps.title: Paint and air-dry

steps.body:
Stir the black vinegar, soy, sugar, chillies, cilantro root and stalks, and garlic until the sugar dissolves.
Let it sit while the chicken roasts so the garlic mellows.
steps.title: Make the Shandong sauce

steps.body:
Heat the oven to 200 °C.
Roast the chicken on baking paper in a roasting pan until the skin is deep mahogany and the thigh reads 82 °C, about 1 hour.
steps.title: Roast

steps.body: Rest the chicken for 15 minutes; it carves cleaner and stays juicy.
steps.title: Rest

steps.body:
Joint the chicken and hand-shred the breast.
Stir a few tablespoons of the rendered fat and pan juices into the sauce, then spoon it over and finish with the chopped cilantro leaves.
steps.title: Carve and dress

summary: Adam Liaw's Shandong chicken gets its crackling skin from an overnight air-dry after a dark soy and Shaoxing glaze. It's carved and dressed with a raw black-vinegar sauce of garlic, bird's eye chilli and cilantro.

why.text: Boiling water shrinks the skin and melts surface fat, so it dries overnight and crisps instead of going leathery.
why.title: Scalding tightens the skin

why.text: Acid makes rich chicken fat taste lighter; sugar and chilli round off the sourness.
why.title: Black vinegar cuts the fat
